a way to get rid of it and to have completely colorless acid but for most applications as far as I know it's not really an issue in any case I reinsulated the adapter and kept collecting the acid I think the distillation took about two hours or so and everything that came over was either at 83 C or slightly below it although 83 C is the boiling point of pure nitric acid I'm definitely not going to be collecting a hundred percent acid the reagents aren't perfectly dry and then I trick acid picks up moisture from the air so the final concentration is usually around 90% as it continued the stuff in the flask slowly dried up and more and more nitrogen dioxide was being produced it eventually looked like there was little to no liquid left and the nitric acid pretty much stopped coming over I think I was getting like one drop every 10 or 15 seconds which just really wasn't worth it so I took away the heating mantle and I ended the distillation the first test they did on the acid was a very simple one and I just blew some air on it this caused a whole bunch of fuming to occur and it's why it's called fuming nitric acid to a certain extent the regular 68-percent acid fumes as well but it isn't nearly as much it only seems to become really significant when it gets above around 80% to measure the yield I poured it into a grad cylinder and I got a volume of about 28 and a half mils then I weighed it and got a mass of 43.1 grams by dividing the mass by the volume I found that had a density of about one point five one I was then able to use a chart that I found online which correlates the density of nitric acid with the concentration so at one point five one grams a mil and room temperature I got that the concentration was between 99 and a hundred percent which was significantly more than I expected another easy test that I think is kind of cool is to combine it with some copper metal nitric acid is one of the few acids that can dissolve copper and it works really well with the regular 68 percent stuff so it's a reasonable assumption that the fuming acid would have an even stronger reaction but oddly enough almost nothing happens this effect is generally known as passivation I looked around but I couldn't find a source that really explained why but this is likely what's happening when the fuming acid attacks the copper it quickly forms a layer of copper oxide on the surface then it slowly converts some of the copper oxide to copper nitrate however copper nitrates practically insoluble in pure nitric acid so as it forms it blocks the acid from attacking more copper oxide and copper metal when waters added though the copper nitrates dissolved away and the protective layer is continually removed all of the reddish orange stuff that you see coming off is nitrogen dioxide gas okay now for the fun part where I see what happens if I get some on my skin and at the same time I figured I'd contrast it with what it can do to gloves so I shot some onto my finger and I had the excess drip onto some pieces of a nitrile glove they very quickly lit on fire but on my finger I didn't feel anything the moment it started to hurt even slightly though I quickly washed off the acid I also kept rinsing my finger for several minutes to make sure that all of it was removed my finger afterwards was stained yellow because the nitric acid reacted with keratin protein in my skin and nail this is pretty typical though with nitric acid and it even happens with the normal lab grade stuff I then soaked it in a solution of just baking soda to make it slightly basic which turned it to more of an orange color there wasn't actually a real purpose in doing this it's not to neutralize the acid or anything I just thought it was kind of interesting in general though I felt like it looked a lot worse than it was the damage was mostly superficial and it didn't even make it past my dead skin layer so as long as it's washed away relatively quickly I feel I can agree that wearing no gloves is probably the better option one thing to keep in mind though is that fingers and hands in general have much thicker skin which really limits the penetration of the acid if I got this on my face or almost anywhere else really the pain probably would have been nearly instantaneous I mean it still wouldn't like my skin on fire but it would definitely cause some serious damage if it weren't dealt with pretty much immediately this is why when I worked with it I made sure to cover my arms and to wear safety glasses I also did it in a fume hood so that my face and upper body were protected behind glass in the lab the two most common glove types are nitrile and latex and I wondered which would be worse to be wearing if you got the acid on it the first run was with the nitrile glove which lit on fire within about three seconds one thing to keep in mind though is that the acid heats up very quickly and it can burn you even before it ignites so the actual amount of time that you have to get it off might be less than three seconds with the latex glove it took about four seconds to ignite which made it seem like it was slightly better however after I put it out and picked it up it's stuck to the dish a bit so although it takes longer to light on fire it might be harder to remove and it could even get stuck on you from this it seems like the latex would be worse the nitrile reacts quicker but it doesn't melt and it might be easier to remove in the end though you should definitely not be wearing either of them just for fun I also tested it on some disposable vinyl gloves I've actually never seen them used in a proper lab before and I rarely use them myself because I finally don't really fit well and they also break easily I honestly expected them to just light on fire like the other ones but the result surprised me I even let it sit there for quite a while and it didn't look like anything was really going on so based on this they might be a viable alternative to working barehanded but I don't really feel comfortable guaranteeing that they're safe for anything as a proper comparison I decided to also include what the 68% acid does it doesn't even come close to lighting it on fire and it also doesn't really heat up however the acid will slowly pass through both nitrile and latex so it should still be removed as soon as possible the last thing that I wanted to show was its use as an oxidant of liquid fuels so I added some kerosene to a small dish put some cotton on top and lit it on fire I then slowly added some of the nitric acid there was an immediate increase in the intensity of the fire and you could hear it as well in some rockets this combination of nitric acid and a fuel is used to propel it I think it would be really cool to make my own little model rocket using nitric acid but we'll see if I ever get around to doing that anyway I think that's about it for now I hope you guys enjoyed the
